title: "Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data"

[Lecture slides](../lectures/04-inspect-archive/lec.qmd) · [Quiz](04-inspect-archive-quiz.qmd) · [Weekly revision](quiz.qmd)


## Which seedlings received the treatment?

A lab group has sent you `lab-data.zip`. Its README says it holds four seedling
pots, two control and two nutrient-treated, each measured once after seven days,
with lengths in millimetres. A table called a **manifest** (`samples.tsv`) lists
each sample's ID, its treatment and the file holding its measurement. Today you
use the terminal to find out which samples were treated and whether they are
longer than the controls.

This is a small, separate practice dataset with four samples; the 24-plant
dataset comes back on day 5 in R. The data are simulated.

**Save today:** `treated-samples.txt`, `working/manifest-practice.tsv` and
`working/observations.txt`, all inside the extracted `lab-data` folder.

## Getting the archive into your workspace

Download [lab-data.zip](../downloads/lab-data.zip) with your browser. The
download lands in your Downloads folder, which is not where your terminal works.
In the terminal, run `cd ~/introcomputing-shell` and then open that folder
graphically with `explorer.exe .` (Ubuntu on Windows) or `open .` (Mac). Copy the
ZIP into it with the file manager, then run `ls` in the terminal: `lab-data.zip`
should be listed.

## What is in the archive?

Use `unzip -l` to find out what the lab group sent before unpacking anything:

```bash
unzip -l lab-data.zip
```

The listing shows eight files: `README.txt`, `samples.tsv`, four measurement files
`measurements/S01.csv` to `S04.csv`, and two short field notes. `-l` only lists;
nothing has been extracted yet. Now extract into a folder of your choice and read
the README:

```bash
unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data
cd lab-data
less README.txt
```

`-d lab-data` names the destination folder. Extraction makes ordinary files you
can open and leaves the ZIP as it was. In `less`, Space moves down and **q**
returns to the prompt.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: `unzip` asks whether to replace a file

You have extracted into `lab-data` before. Answer `n`, look at the existing folder
in the file manager, and extract into a fresh name such as `lab-data-2` instead.
Then use that name in `cd`.
:::

## How many samples are there?

Use `head` and `wc -l` to find out how many samples the manifest describes:

```bash
head -n 3 samples.tsv
wc -l samples.tsv
```

`head -n 3` shows the first three lines: a header naming the columns
(`sample_id`, `treatment`, `file`), then S01 and S02. `wc -l` counts lines and
prints **5**: one header plus **four** samples. The columns are separated by tabs,
which is what TSV (tab-separated values) means; a CSV uses commas.

## Which samples were treated?

Use `grep` to find out which samples received the treatment:

```bash
grep -F treated samples.tsv
```

`grep` prints every line that contains the search text; `-F` means plain text,
not a pattern. You should see two lines, **S03** and **S04**. The header and the
control lines do not contain the word, so they are not printed.

`grep` matches text, not meaning: a line saying `untreated` would also match,
because it contains `treated`. Always look at the lines it selected, not only
at how many there are.

## Saving and counting the treated samples

Save the treated lines to a file, and count them with a pipe:

```bash
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt
less treated-samples.txt
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
```

`>` sends the output into `treated-samples.txt` instead of the screen. The
manifest is read and stays unchanged. The vertical bar `|` is a **pipe**: it
passes grep's lines straight to `wc -l`, which prints **2**.

`>` replaces whatever the destination file contained before, so never put the
input file after it: `grep … samples.tsv > samples.tsv` can empty the manifest
before grep reads it.

## Are the treated seedlings longer?

The manifest's `file` column says where each measurement is. Use `head` on those
files to find out how long the treated and control seedlings were:

```bash
head measurements/S03.csv
head measurements/S04.csv
head measurements/S01.csv
head measurements/S02.csv
```

Each file has one header line and one value. The treated seedlings are
**42.4 mm** (S03) and **39.8 mm** (S04); the controls are **32.1 mm** (S01) and
**35.2 mm** (S02). Both treated seedlings are longer than both controls. With
two pots per group that is a hint, not a result; the 24-plant dataset in week 2
is where we start answering the question properly.

## A practice copy of the manifest

You will want a copy of the manifest you can change without risking the
original. Make one in a `working` folder and give it a clearer name:

```bash
mkdir working
cp samples.tsv working/samples-copy.tsv
mv working/samples-copy.tsv working/manifest-practice.tsv
ls working
ls
```

`cp` makes a second file; `mv` renames (or moves) it. `ls working` shows only
`manifest-practice.tsv`, and `ls` shows that the original `samples.tsv` is still
there. Both `cp` and `mv` silently replace an existing file with the destination
name, so check names first.

Then use the file manager to create `working/observations.txt` with your answers
from today: how many samples there are and why `wc -l` says 5, which two were
treated, their lengths, and which file holds S04's measurement.

## When `untreated` also matches

A colleague's version of the manifest labels S01 as `untreated` instead of
`control`. Use your practice copy to find out what `grep -F treated` selects then.

1. Copy `working/manifest-practice.tsv` to `working/search-trap.tsv`. Open only
   this copy in a text editor and change S01's `control` to `untreated`.
2. Predict, then run `grep -F treated working/search-trap.tsv | wc -l`.

The count is **3**: S01, S03 and S04. `untreated` contains the text `treated`, so
grep cannot tell the two labels apart. Running `grep -F treated working/search-trap.tsv`
without the count shows you the S01 line and makes the problem visible. The
original `samples.tsv` still gives 2.

## A measurement file that seems to be missing

When you receive data, every file the manifest names should exist. Use a copy of
the folder to find out what you see when one has been renamed.

1. In the file manager, copy the whole `lab-data` folder to `received-check`.
   In `received-check/measurements`, rename `S04.csv` to `S04-renamed.csv`.
2. In the terminal, `cd` into `received-check` and try
   `head measurements/S04.csv`. It fails with *No such file or directory*,
   although the manifest still lists that path.
3. Use `ls measurements` and `head measurements/S04-renamed.csv` to find out
   which sample that file holds. It contains `S04,39.8`, the S04 measurement.
4. Because you know it is S04, restore the name with
   `mv measurements/S04-renamed.csv measurements/S04.csv` and check that
   `head measurements/S04.csv` works again.

In real data, a file whose identity you cannot confirm from its contents is a
question for the lab group, not something to rename by guessing. Add the
problem, the evidence and the repair to `working/observations.txt`.

## Which samples are esters? (an organic-laboratory inventory)

This optional task uses the same commands on a different archive: a simulated
inventory of four organic-chemistry samples, each with a supplied class label.
No chemistry knowledge is needed.

Download [organic-lab.zip](../downloads/organic-lab.zip), copy it into
`~/introcomputing-shell` with the file manager as above, and use the day's
commands to find out which samples are labelled `ester` and how many there are:

```bash
cd ~/introcomputing-shell
unzip -l organic-lab.zip
unzip organic-lab.zip -d organic-lab
cd organic-lab
less README.txt
grep -F ester inventory.tsv > ester-samples.txt
grep -F ester inventory.tsv | wc -l
```

The inventory has a header and four samples. Two match: **O02** and **O03**.
grep searched the supplied labels; it does not recognise chemical structures.
The archive also contains `organic-recovery.csv`, which you will use for
calculations later in the course.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Did `grep` change the manifest? Why does `wc -l` count 5 for four samples?

`grep` only reads the manifest; `>` wrote its output to a separate file.
`wc -l` counts lines, and the manifest has one header line plus four sample lines.
The saved `treated-samples.txt` has no header, because the header did not match.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why list a ZIP with `unzip -l` before extracting it?

You see what you received, and the folder structure it will create, before any
files are written. If something is missing, you can ask the sender straight away.
:::

**Save today:** `treated-samples.txt`, `working/manifest-practice.tsv` and
`working/observations.txt` in the extracted `lab-data` folder, and keep
`lab-data.zip` unchanged.
